utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Before we go into anything, shall we go into private session first. There's one matter I'd like to deal with in the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session. Mr. Tieger, you wanted to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you very much. I wanted to advise the Chamber that one of the witnesses affected by yesterday's decision, KDZ477, was scheduled for next week. We will attempt to substitute, at least during the course of next week, not necessarily in the same precise time-frame, Witness KDZ244. I wanted to alert the Defence and the Chamber to that effort. And we'll, of course, alert the Court if there are any scheduling difficulties in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is 477 a protected witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was trying to recall. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say thank you for these documents. They are not corps documents, they are police documents, so we'll probably have them all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. There may be one matter I will raise at the end of today's session that may affect the future witness scheduling. We'll see. If the witness would kindly take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours; good afternoon, Mr. Witness. Mr. Registrar, 65 ter 90201, please, and this should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, without reading it out, can you confirm that that is your name on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Can this, please, be admitted under seal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1903, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, as discussed, your evidence in this case is going to be submitted in writing, so let me address the formalities associated with that submission. Mr. Registrar, 65 ter 90200, please. And, again, this should not be broadcast. Mr. Witness, you have previously provided statements to the Prosecution, and you have also testified in the cases of Dragomir Milosevic and Momcilo Perisic. Now, looking at the screen in front of you, do you see your signature at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review this statement before appending your signature to it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And does the document accurately reflect the evidence you have previously given the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Finally, if you were examined on the same topics today, would you provide the same information to the Court?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I request the admission of this statement, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you minded to produce a public version with redaction?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. In keeping with our previous practice, we shall provide a public version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll give them a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 90200 will be Exhibit P1904 under seal, and the public redacted version will be Exhibit P1905.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: The following is a summary of the evidence contained in that statement: Witness 485 worked as a homicide inspector for the Sarajevo Security Services from around April 1994 until the end of the conflict. In this role, he participated in the investigation of shelling and sniping incidents. He attended so many incidents of shelling and sniping that he cannot remember how many he investigated. His role in the on-site investigation team was to ensure that the crime scene was secured and that each team member, which included forensic technicians and ballistic experts, executed their role. And observations and information obtained during this preliminary investigation were included in an official report. Among other investigations, the witness investigated four scheduled incidents: Incident F-11, the firing on a passenger tram on 8 October 1994; Incident G9, the shelling of Bascarsija Flea Market on 22nd December 1994; G-13, the use of a modified air-bomb in Safeta Hadzica Street on 26 May 1994; and G-19, the shelling of Markale Market on 28 August 1995. In each instance, the on-site investigation identified the origin of the fire as Bosnian Serb-held territory. And that concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I now have some additional questions for the witness. Turning, firstly, to Scheduled Incident F-11, and if I could have 65 ter 09673, please. Once again, this document should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, this is a report dated 10th of October, 1994, and it concerns the firing on a tram on the 8th of October, 1994. Without reading it out, does your name appear as one of the participants in the investigation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 2 of the English, leaving the B/C/S where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: At the bottom of both versions, it states that: "Four entry holes were made by bullets. This was most probably caused by the so-called 'Sijac Smrti,'" which is here translated as a "Death Sower." Mr. Witness, what type of weapon, to your knowledge, was known as a "Death Sower?"

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: What I know, although I am not an expert in fire-arms, it's a submachine-gun that fired rounds at very high velocity, and I heard people saying that anyone who found themselves in the cross-hairs of such a weapon was unable to run away quickly enough because the gun fired so quickly, and that's why it got the nickname "Death Sower."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Can this document please be admitted under seal. Again, the Prosecution is minded to also provide public redacted versions of each of these associated exhibits in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayden. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1906 under seal, and the public redacted version will be Exhibit P1907.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: 65 ter 09906, please, Mr. Registrar, and turning to Scheduled Incident G-19.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, had you ever visited the Markale Market area prior to or during the month of August 1995?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Yes. I went to that part of Sarajevo and the market before the war and after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Can you describe briefly what you observed at the Markale Market or the area of the Markale Market on any typical day?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: It's a market-place where people buy and sell all sorts of products, including meat and dairy products. One part of the market is closed, and the other part is in the open air. What you could observe at any time before the war, during the war, and after the war was that many civilians gathered and concentrated in that and similar places because they needed to buy things for their own needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And do these observations include the alleyways around Markale Market, itself?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you participated in the investigation of the shelling of Markale Market on 28 August 1995, and you wrote the report that we see in front of us. That report states that your team arrived on the scene at 12.15 p.m., approximately one and a quarter hours after the explosion. Can you briefly describe what you found, arriving on the scene?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: I'm trying to find that passage, because I can't see the beginning of the report on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If we might move to page 2 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I see in this report, it is correct that we arrived at 1215 hours. And my first impression, my first observation, was that officers from the local Police Administration had sealed off the site, meaning that they closed access to the very spot hit by the projectile, and they closed all the alleyways leading to the site. And when we arrived to one of those main streets -- to the main street, which is one of the main streets in Sarajevo, you could see a lot of personal items scattered around, items that had belonged to the casualties, shards of glass, fragments on the surrounding buildings, but it was immediately obvious that there were no bodies of anyone killed or anyone wounded. That is what I was able to see at the first moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: You mentioned that there were no bodies of killed or wounded. Was this typical when you arrived on the scene of a shelling or sniping incident you investigated?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Yes. In most cases where I did the on-site investigation, that was the rule. We usually did not find any of the casualties still lying there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And in your view, why was it that both the wounded as well as the deceased bodies were moved from these scenes almost immediately after the incident?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Well, surviving eye-witnesses or anyone who happened to be there at the time of the explosion, without even checking whether any of the people lying there were still alive or not, rushed to move them, by any transport vehicle available, to the hospital, probably also because there was rarely a doctor around who would carry out the triage, to see who was dead, who was seriously wounded, or who was lightly wounded, or who would be able to assign any priorities in transporting people to the hospital. Even when the ambulance arrived, the physician and the paramedics who came with the ambulance were able to take perhaps one person to the hospital. The rest was up to the passersby. That's what I think, and that's what I also heard from other people while conducting my business. That's the main reason why casualties and the dead were taken away before the on-site investigation team arrived. And also the interval between the explosion and our arrival was more than one hour. I don't think that even the bodies of the dead, let alone those injured, should have been left waiting for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Turning to page 2 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S, at the end of the report, Mr. Witness, it indicates that 35 persons were killed and 78 wounded, and that lists of the victims and killed are attached to the report. Did you participate in the identification of these listed persons?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Yes, I did. This is mainly data that we got then. I don't know if this is the final number of those killed, 35. It's hard for me to remember. It's been a long time ago. I don't remember if anyone who was seriously wounded in the meantime died from sustained injuries in hospital, but this is the initial data that we were able to get initially at the medical institution; to be precise, in the two hospitals, the State Hospital and the former Military Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And when you went to these two hospitals and compiled this list, how could you tell that these persons were killed or wounded as a result of the explosion at Markale Market, as opposed to some other cause of death or injury?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Most of them had their identification documents with them, and we were able to establish their identity on the basis of their IDs that they had on them. Another source of information were their relatives, closer or more distant relatives, who also provided information regarding those who were killed or wounded. So these were sources for the identification of those persons. Naturally, we got some information also from the medical personnel, who also got their information in the same way. So it was either us or together with the medical personnel who got this information about the persons in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: You've identified how you were able to ID the bodies or the wounded persons. I'm also interested as to how you were able to link the death or injury of these persons to the Markale Market explosion. How could you tell that they had been killed or wounded in that explosion?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: When we came to the hospital, we went to the place where the wounded are admitted and we also went to the morgue. At both those places -- actually, in the morgue, we met the forensic experts, who told us -- who confirmed for us that the persons that I listed here as killed from the explosion -- said that all of them had blast injuries, injuries from fragments of the explosive device. Regardless of what this forensics expert confirmed for us, we, ourselves -- I mean, I went to so many investigations on-scene. This also applied to the judge as well as those present from the United Nations. We could all see that these were blast injuries, and they are definitely very different types of injuries from injuries caused by projectiles fired from a fire-arm. So even I, as a layperson, was able to see that these were really people who were hurt in the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I tender the document in front of us as an exhibit under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1908, under seal, Your Honours. And the public redacted version will be Exhibit P1909.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Witness, aside from the incidents that I described in your summary before, did the shelling incidents that you investigated in 1994 and 1995 generally involve fatalities?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: For the most part, yes. I belonged to the Homicide Department, or murders, so this is what kind of investigations on-scene I and my colleagues carried out. We would go out to investigate on the scene when a person was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And did that include civilian fatalities?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Regardless of what kind of a victim it was, what I did and what I wrote about -- actually, my reports mostly had to deal with civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And when you arrived to investigate a fatality, did you take steps to determine whether there had been military activity in the area immediately prior to the incident you were investigating? And if so, what steps were those?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Before we would go to the scene, we would usually get in touch -- actually, we would usually be informed by the local police, the police officers in the location, what the security situation was and if the conditions existed for us to go out there safely, arrive across town safely, and what the situation was at the scene. The local police officers were our source for that kind of information, and, of course, we would gather information from them, if there was any kind of combat action underway at the point in time when the incident occurred for which they were requesting an on-scene investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And in your view, were the civilian fatalities that you investigated generally the result of military exchanges, what is commonly referred to as "collateral damage"?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: A large majority of the fatalities in the events that I investigated were casualties that occurred outside of any type of military activity. When I say "military activity," I mean fighting between the warring parties. Usually -- I mean, Sarajevo is not a large town, so if there was any fighting, people knew that very well. They had learned how to live in such conditions. So whenever any kind of combat action is sensed, very few or practically no civilians were out in the streets or in places where they would be exposed to fire. Therefore, in those investigations that I took part in, these people were not collateral damage; they were the actual victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: At this stage, I tender the remaining associated exhibits. I note that since filing the notification, none of the 65 ter numbers have become exhibits, so it's just those that were already listed with their exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of particular interest would be those investigation reports signed and authenticated by the witness. There are four other reports: 9688, 9769, 9821, and 9921. All that witness did in previous proceedings is that he authenticated them. So in that regard, I have some question whether it would form an indispensable and inseparable part of this transcript, but not as an indispensable and inseparable part of this previous statement, but on the basis of the witness's answer given today, that he would have given the same answers had he been examined again, so we take it that he authenticated it today, so on that basis I think we can admit them, unless they are objected to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any other objections? So your intention is to produce all the investigation reports and other exhibits, to produce a public version of them with proper redaction?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: That's right, they should all be admitted under seal, and we will produce a public version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. With that understanding, they will be all admitted, and the proper exhibit numbers will be circulated by the Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just before you start your examination, I'd like to remind you that whenever we are to discuss any information which may reveal the witness's identity, we should go into private session. Bear that in mind, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So far, it went well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And whenever you may feel that any question and any answers you may give may reveal your identity, please ask for the private session, please, before you answer, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I hope everything went well so far, and also we have half an hour delay, so the witness need not be overly concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, first of all, I would like to ask you, sir, why you are so committed to the protective measures.

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: I don't know how relevant that is. I stated my reasons, they were accepted, so I really wouldn't like to explain why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You don't have to. If you'd like to discuss it, we should go into private session, first of all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go into private session briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the Court has already ruled on this. The representations have been made by the witness to the Prosecution, and he's confirmed those representations today. I'm not sure there is any further information that will change the Chamber's ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are in private session? No. The Chamber made it clear that the previous protective measures would continue, but I take it Mr. Karadzic is not -- I take it that Mr. Karadzic is not asking for the variation of protective measures, and the Chamber is of the view he may be entitled to put some questions in relation to those protective measures to test the credibility of the witness. But as a matter of practicality, I'm not sure whether there would be many points on that. If you would like to put some questions, we need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Chamber's assessment of my intentions or gauging of my intentions is absolutely correct. Can we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for your contact with the Defence team and with me via videolink. This helped us a little bit to go a little bit faster through a number of circumstances, because we have a number of incidents that are going to require a lot of time. We agreed during the interview -- you informed us that you carried out many investigations and that you did not keep records of that, so that you don't know the number, but that there are records of that in the MUP archives. That's what you believe; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Yes, I said that I did not have a private diary, I didn't keep a private diary, but I did write reports about what I did and where I went. And in the same way that this Court and this OTP has records, in the same way the records of my work should be in the police archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the investigations were carried out according to the provisions of the then enforced Law on Criminal Procedure and Rules of Service, and that you only could find some, perhaps, comments or something lacking in these reports because they were done in wartime circumstances?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: It's correct that the investigations were carried out according to the laws and the Rules of Service at the time, and I said that if there are any errors or anything that is unclear in my reports, it's possible that this happened only because of the circumstances in which we were doing our work; the war conditions, primarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How would that circumstance affect your reports?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Could you be more specific? Which circumstance? So far, it hasn't been said that an error had been found that I was not able to explain. If you have something specific in mind, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you said that the possibility of repeated fire on the site resulted in hasty work, which might explain any deficiencies in investigative actions?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: One of the reasons why an error could possibly occur -- I said "possibly," but if you have a specific error in mind that needs to be explained, or some deficiency in my report, please put it to me and I'll try to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many times did it happen, Witness, that the crime scene was hit again while the investigation was ongoing? If I can help you, look at item 8 in your amalgamated statement, where you say that: "At times, it was a problem. It was risky to perform our procedures. There was always a possibility for the location to be fired at again." How many times, out of the countless investigations you conducted, did it happen that a location was hit again during investigation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you have your statement in front of you, or can you answer the question without having to see your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer the question, and the answer is very brief. I said, even in the statement, that there was a possibility. I didn't say it ever happened. It didn't actually happen to us. But why was there a possibility? Because our chiefs told us that our radio traffic was susceptible to listening, to eavesdropping, and that the enemy might hear what we were doing and where. So I didn't say that it happened. I said there was a possibility, and we were warned about that possibility. And we tried to finish our work in the open air as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But did those who fired the initial shell that was being investigated have the possibility of seeing that an important team had arrived, and since the MUP had arrived, the target could be profitable? And how is it possible, then, that in hundreds of cases, it never happened that they fired a shell again and thus killed people who could have been a profitable target?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: I don't know whether I ever confirmed or said anywhere that I, as a policeman, participated in any military activities. Neither I nor my colleagues from my department, or other departments of the criminal investigation police, ever participated in military activities. I only said we used our own radio communications, and we were warned that our radio traffic might be eavesdropped on, and that our location could be discovered at any time. Considering the circumstances prevailing in Sarajevo and how encircled it was, whether somebody was able to look at us, to observe us, or to listen to us, it's quite certain that it was a possibility, but I cannot positively answer whether somebody from their position was able to see us or establish visual contact well enough to see that we were the police, especially since I was always wearing civilian clothes, I had no police markings, and I said that I belonged to the part of the civilian police that worked in "Mufti." Whether somebody could have watched us while we were working, I really don't know and I can't give you a positive answer. That they were able to eavesdrop, they were. Anyone who knew the city and the streets in the city could have a very good idea of where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please don't feel offended or defensive. If somebody who fired already and knows where they fired - they have the trig point - they can expect well that there will be a lot of people concentrating there very soon. Have you heard ever that a single investigator got killed from such repeated fire?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: I said already that it never happened to me, personally, but we had been warned about such a possibility. I am not aware that any of my colleagues died in precisely those circumstances, but I cannot say positively that such things did not happen. It's just that I'm not aware of any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to paragraph 10 in your statement, where you say that the direction of fire was determined in cases of shelling, and you said in our interview that the distance could not be determined.

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Not when we talked, no. I did not say, when we talked, that the distance could not be determined. Speaking about that, what I said was that the direction from which the projectile was fired was determined by the bomb squad team and ballistics team. I wrote in my report whatever they told me on that subject. I was not the person who determined the direction, or claimed that a projectile came from that location or another location, or that it was possible or impossible to determine it. I just said that it was not part of my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But did they do their job according to procedure?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Again, I don't think it's a good question for me. I am not an expert. I don't know much about the methods they use, the aids they use, the tables they use. I don't know these things. And I didn't interfere much with their work, if I can put it that way. For me, it was sufficient that they give me a preliminary estimate that a projectile had landed from such and such a direction, plus/minus 5 degrees, that's how it usually went, and I put that in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at paragraph 6 of your statement. That's what I mean. It says there that you made sure that all members of the team did their job properly, and that's what I'm asking you. Did you make sure that they did their job properly? Now, tell me, Witness, in paragraph 11 you said, very honestly, that there were not many ballistics experts available. How did it go when there was no ballistics experts around? Who did that part of the work? You can feel free to use your statement. It's paragraph 11.

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: If I may go back to what you asked me, you asked first about paragraph 6. I said my job was to provide the right conditions for them to do their job properly, and to make sure they're not interfered with. When I said there was a shortage of ballistics experts, there is some truth in that. However, if it happened that ballistics experts were unable to come to a particular crime scene, especially in incidents where it was possible for CID technicians to determine the direction of fire, then they did it, because they had training as part of their job. In easier incidents, where it was easier to determine the direction of fire, scenes-of-crimes officers from the Criminal Investigation Department did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did they do it at the scene or in their offices?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: I can only remember one such incident where one person was killed and ballistics experts were unable to come, and in that case only the SOCO, the scene-of-crime officer, determined the fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In all other cases, it was the ballistics experts?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: It was, in all incidents that I can remember, the ballistics expert or the bomb squad expert. There's only one case that I remember when the ballistics expert was absent, and that was gun-fire and sniping in Dobrinja settlement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Those other things concerning the trams and the sites we'll deal with later when we come to specific incidents. You said during the interview that your report alone would be insufficient for court purposes.

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: You have to make yourself clearer. What do you mean? What do you mean, it would be insufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I asked you, Would a report like yours be sufficient for you to appear before a court in Bosnia? You said that just with that report, you would not be unable -- you would be unable to do anything before the Court in Bosnia. It's just part of a broader material.

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: I, alone, would not be doing anything with my report. Somebody would have to assess my report, and that would be the person presenting the case to the Court. I said my report was just one of the many documents the Court received. In addition to my report, there were reports of everyone else who was part of the team; first of all, the report of the scene-of-crimes officer, the ballistic report and the bomb squad report. My report was just one of the attachments to the criminal report that was sent to the prosecutor's office. And how worthy or unworthy my report was, I am not the best person to estimate. It was up to the prosecutor to determine how solid it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in your statement that you would wait for others to give you their reports, and then you made yours. Is it then the case that your report is some sort of synthesis?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: I'd like to see that statement where I allegedly said I waited for other reports. No, I did not say that. I said I wrote my report. That was sent to a department, which at that time was called the Genocide Department, and they collected all the other reports. My report was only my report, describing what preceded my arrival at the scene, what I found at the scene, and what I saw; nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll find that. It's somewhere in the amalgamated statement and in your prior evidence. Now, did the BH Army have so-called "Death Sowers"?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So if you mention a Death Sower, your first thought would be the Bosnian Serb side?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: I would not have any thoughts of any side. I just told you I'm not aware whether the BH Army had that weapon. I just told you that in one incident, it seemed to have been used by the other side, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of the Interior know whether Death Sowers were available to the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: I'm not the right person to ask this question. I told you that I had no contact with -- in my work with the army or members of the army, because I did strictly police work, work that was within the purview of the Homicide Department.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get 1D429 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I ask you: Where is the dental clinic?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Somewhere close to a place called Bjelave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that where you lived, in that part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: I lived in a part of Sarajevo called Dijelove [as interpreted] -- sorry, Bjelave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm this format and the person who signed this? Chief of the Security Services Centre, Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: I cannot recognise the form. I wasn't in a position to look at documents like this, especially since I can see it's marked as "Secret" or "Confidential." So this was not accessible to me. I do know the person who signed the document. He was my chief for a while.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at the next page, please. For the others to know, because we don't have information, this is information of the 19th of October, 1993, and the chief of the Security Services is informing his superiors about the conduct of the 11th Independent Battalion of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina located in Mese Selimovica Street; more precisely, in the ground-floor premises of the School of Dentistry of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that that is the first sentence?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Yes, that is the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can't really manage the rest, but it says at the bottom: "In front of the sighted bunker, there is a concrete slab, 30 by 10 metres, on which four vehicles are parked, two ambulances, as well as one an armoured combat vehicle. This vehicle is very interesting because ..." Can we look at the next page. "... because there is a guard with a machine-gun inside it, a so-called 'Death Sower'." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: I really wasn't able to follow you. I'm trying to find where that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first sentence at the top: "This vehicle was very interesting for the reason that there was a guard in it with a machine-gun called the 'Death Sower'."

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: At the top, I can just see the end of that sentence. Probably, the beginning is on the previous page, but that's probably what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Somewhere in the middle, I'm going to read: "Members of the said unit have been boasting how they have 13 machine-guns, Death Sowers, as well as no one can do anything to them." They're also mentioning two nitroglycerine rifles. It's somewhere towards the middle of the page, where it says "2 STMB."

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I'm correct, this is the clinic, and between it and the Medical Faculty, there was the former Nemanjina Street; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we tender this document, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may just add that, from whatever I was able to see, this is a document from 1993. I would just like to draw your attention to the fact that I was not in town at the time and I was not living in the part of town called Bjelave at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, but you are not the problem here but the Death Sowers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless it is objected to, we'll mark it for identification pending translation. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wanted to raise a general matter with respect to the documents that are being marked for identification. I raised this with Mr. Robinson earlier. I had noted the increasing number of documents that are not translated, and so I inquired about the process for attempting to ensure, to the extent possible, that there are translations when documents are presented. I understand that that effort has essentially been abandoned by the Defence, and we have no longer any realistic expectation of receiving translations for documents -- well, other than those that may already be up-loaded in the e-court -- and that would even include documents that have been translated, are available on EDS, but will not be identified as such when presented in court. I raise that not to necessarily revisit the issue. We've been attempting to cope with it as well as possible, but I think the problem is -- the problem that it creates, as we're attempting to assimilate the significance of a document on the spot, are obvious. And in addition, I raise it because I want to ensure that when translations finally come back, that that does not mean the automatic admission of the document, because it will still be incumbent on us then to finally review the document once we finally have the opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. You beat the Chamber in raising this. The Chamber was waiting for a moment to raise this concern. It's imperative for the Defence to prepare the English translation well in advance, while understanding the difficulties preparing for the Defence. It's time-consuming when we deal with any untranslated document. We'll come to that issue later on. We give the number for this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D858.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we'll have a break for 25 minutes and resume at five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It would really be good to dwell a little bit on the matter of translations and also on the resources of the Defence, and perhaps at the first opportunity we could place this on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There is a matter the Chamber wishes to deal with in the absence of the witness. It's sort of an oral ruling. The Chamber is seized of the accused's 26th motion for finding of disclosure violation and for remedial measures, which makes reference to the disclosure of an additional 14.276 pages of documents by the Prosecution on 13th and 22nd October 2010 pursuant to Rule 68. A decision on whether this amounts to a disclosure violation will be issued in due course, along with the decisions on the pending 22nd and 24th motions for finding of disclosure violations. Irrespective of whether the disclosure of this substantial quantity of material at this stage constitutes a violation of the Prosecution's obligation to disclose potentially exculpatory material to the accused on an ongoing basis, and as soon as practicable after such material comes into the Prosecution's possession, the Chamber is of the view that the sheer volume of this material is such that it is in the interests of justice to suspend the proceedings temporarily. This is to allow the accused and his team time to conduct the necessary review of the material and, where appropriate, make use of it in his ongoing cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses and preparations for the Defence phase of the case. The Chamber reminds the accused that it is his task, as lead counsel in his own Defence team, to properly organise and co-ordinate the review of this material, and to prioritise documents which seem most pertinent to upcoming witnesses. The period of time given for the review is not premised on a calculation of the time necessary to conduct a detailed examination of all the documents, but rather, on the time required to assess the material, as a whole, and identify those which must be given the most immediate attention. In determining the period of suspension, the Chamber also takes into consideration the significant number of violations by the Prosecution of its disclosure obligation under 66(A)(ii) and Rule 68 which have been found to date. While, individually, it may be said that the accused has not suffered prejudice by the late disclosure of certain documents, the Chamber is increasingly troubled by the potential cumulative effect of such late disclosure. The Chamber reminds the Prosecution that the size and complexity of this case is not an excuse for its failure to properly organise itself to ensure that disclosure is carried out in accordance with the Rules. Indeed, in the pre-trial phase the Prosecution was urged to reduce the scope of the case, or to find ways to divide it into more manageable pieces, in the interests of a fair and expeditious trial. The Prosecution represented that it was ready for trial in 2009, but apparently ensuring that it had fully complied with the dead-lines set by the Pre-Trial Judge for disclosure was not fully reflected in that assertion. The Chamber, therefore, reiterates that the Prosecution - I mean the Office of the Prosecutor as a whole - must take seriously its disclosure obligations and ensure that all necessary resources are dedicated to ensuring timely disclosure of material to this accused, as, indeed, to all other accused at this Tribunal. Taking all these factors into account, the Chamber finds that it is necessary to suspend the trial proceedings for a period of one month, as soon as possible. We will finish hearing the witnesses scheduled for this week. We will also hear evidence next week from those witnesses who are already in The Hague or who are already in transit. Thereafter, we shall suspend the proceedings for a month, and resume on a date and time to be notified to the parties. Therefore, Mr. Tieger, we expect you to advise us, by tomorrow morning, which witnesses we will thus hear from next week. We are also cognisant of the fact that there are certain witnesses scheduled for later this month whose evidence is locked in to particular dates. We hope that you will make your best efforts to reschedule them. However, should there be one whose evidence is scheduled for sometime in this period whom it is impossible to reschedule, we will consider hearing the evidence of that witness on the currently scheduled date, so long as you advise us in writing by close of business on Wednesday, 10th of November, who that witness is and why, despite your best efforts, he or she cannot be rescheduled. Should it be necessary to hear such a witness, the Chamber will consider the impact thereof on the end-date for that period of suspension. That's the oral ruling, and we'll bring in the witness again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to express my gratitude and -- gratitude for your understanding. But I'm just wondering if perhaps the Prosecution doesn't wish to be rid of this case by bringing us into such a position that the case could be dismissed before the beginning of the case defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just want to -- I don't want to respond. I just hope the Court appreciates that I don't rise to the bait of such outlandish statements and provocation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we would have been very surprised if you had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we open the blinds. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, I would like to go through a small part or number of your investigations as soon as possible. Did you take part in the investigation of the shelling of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina building on the 8th of December, 1994?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: I can't remember now. If you do have that report, perhaps you would be kind enough to show it to me and then I confirm it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at 1D2721 without broadcasting it outside, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Until then: Witness, did the CSB treat in the same way all the incidents where, for example, there was civilian casualties or civilian buildings were hit, and did they differentiate such incidents from those that suffered damage in fighting?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: As far as I know, we treated all incidents in the same way, and we acted or worked in the same way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 1 of this document. Perhaps it's a good thing that you saw the signature. Can we make sure that this is not broadcast, then. Anyway, can we look at page 1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the CSB differentiate between civilian targets and legitimate military targets?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: As far as I know, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It conducted exactly the same investigations in the case of civilian targets and legitimate military targets; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: As far as I know, when I went for investigations, and from what I could see, we treated all incidents in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Other than the first person on the list, can you please tell me the training or the qualifications of each of these people on the list? Let's say number 2, what was the education?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Higher Administrative College.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Go on. 3?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: I think he was a graduate of law school. As for number 4 and number 5, I really couldn't tell. I don't know. I'm not able to tell you, either, for 7 or 8, number 9 -- no, no, I really couldn't tell you what the education of the others was, or their qualifications. I can only say it for 2 or 3, because I know that myself for a fact. I don't know about the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, the person under number 2, why is that person qualified or on what grounds are they able to be the head of the criminal investigations team, with or without the presence of the investigation judge?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Well, his training, education, and his experience qualify him for that job, and, of course, fulfilling the terms that are set for that particular post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us, Administrative School is a school for administrative personnel; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: In the diploma which you get after you graduate from that school, you are granted the title of administrative lawyer. So you are not a graduated lawyer but an administrative lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that this team investigated this incident of the 8th of December, 1994, when a section of the Presidency building was hit? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Yes, this was the team that went to the site and conducted an investigation there. I don't see that it says in my report that they conducted the complete investigation. It just says that the on-scene investigation team went and did their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember which part of the building was struck?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: I'm trying to find that here in my report and to confirm that, but I think that this was a part that is facing Trebevic, that is, the southern side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph beginning: "By inspecting the scene of the incident ...," this is the fourth paragraph after the names, is it true that the struck kitchen premises of the Ministry of Defence area is located at the southern side of the Presidency building? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then does this make the building a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Well, I'm not the person who would be able to determine what is a legitimate military target and what isn't. Probably there is somebody who could make that evaluation, but these were -- this was a part where the administrative area of the Ministry of Defence was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the rest of his answer, and could Mr. Karadzic repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters couldn't hear the last part of your answer, Mr. Witness. You stopped, in terms of interpretation: "But there were -- this was a part where the administrative area of the Ministry of Defence was." Did you say anything else from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that that's from what I know was the administrative part of the building, and that at the time when I was there, I didn't see -- well, I saw that it was a kitchen, that it was being used by the Ministry of Defence, but I didn't see any armed soldiers in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you did see that it was a kitchen, and you knew that it was the Ministry of Defence kitchen, just as it says in the report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: It states in the report that that was a kitchen that was being used, not that it's their property. So they were using it, they were probably coming there, but I don't know that this belongs to them. I just wrote that it was being used by them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D2629, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can I ask you to confirm or deny that this is a document by the president of the Presidency, who is writing a letter to the prime minister, in which he said: "You promised that you were going to free up some rooms in the Presidency buildings, and nothing came of that." And then he says: "We're only using 30 per cent, three salons, and at the same time the government in the same building is using 150 rooms." And then it says -- you can look at this part here, where it says: "There is another problem. The Chetniks are shooting at the Presidency building and are constantly stating that they are doing that because the Ministry of Defence is located there. They know it. It doesn't matter what the Chetniks say, but this is something that UNPROFOR is telling us as well. As far they're concerned, this is a military facility. Also, the building has been entered in the Registry of Cultural Monuments, and such buildings, according to The Hague Convention and according to our laws, should not have anything in them that would constitute a military target, and that is why, when you're considering relocating, the first thing that should be relocated would be the Ministry of Defence. In town, allegedly, there are two more buildings, the property of the republic, which, for unknown reasons, have not been taken over. One of them is in Dositejeva Street, 20 offices, and the second one is in the Kesovanija Street, 40 offices. And the second one in the Kesovanija Street, 40 offices." And so on and so forth. Is that the signature by Mr. Izetbegovic, the late Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Well, I was never in a position to see documents that were signed by the president of the Presidency, so I really can't tell whether this is an original document or not. I cannot confirm its authenticity. All I can say is that I am familiar with the name Dr. Haris Silajdzic and the name of the late president, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. I didn't have the opportunity of receiving any document directly from him, so I really never saw any document that he, himself, signed personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But this corresponds to what you said and what you reported yourself, that there were some parts of the Ministry of Defence there. And he even says that the whole Defence Ministry is situated in the Presidency building and that the government has taken many rooms in that building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: You can see from the document that it confirms what I said earlier, that we treated all the incidents in the same way and that I just wrote down what I actually saw. I didn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're tendering the previous document as well?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not necessary, that's not necessary. I do not want to overburden the list of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I'd only note, in that respect, that the line of questioning presumes that you have the document in front of you to be able to understand it, so it may be prudent to admit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless it is objected to by you, we'll admit both of them, marking them for identification, both of them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 1D2721 will be MFI D859, and 1D2629 will be MFI D860.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you take part in the investigation where a girl was killed in Dobrinja, I believe, on the 14th or 15th of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: I've already mentioned that I did attend one such on-site investigation. But whether it was on exactly that very day, I would very much appreciate if you could tell me where I can find it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have 65 ter 09766, the first page. This should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, does this assist you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Yes, and I did attend this on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who carried out the ballistics examination?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: The forensic technician, the crime-of-scene [as interpreted] officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the official report was drafted by you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you accepted his report and integrated it here, or was it a separate report that was attached to yours?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: As I've already mentioned on a number of occasions, I integrated into my report all the information that I obtained on site, and later on he would prepare his own report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please confirm that this incident was at Nehruova Street, number 10? Today, the name of that street is Hamdije Kapidzica; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: As for Dobrinja and its various parts, I really am not very familiar with that part of the town. I wasn't really familiar with it before the war, let alone during the war. And if I noted in the report that it was Nehruova Street, then that refers to its name from that time. What its new name is, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we do have that new name and the list of new street names. It is Hamdije Kapidzica Street. Can you now tell us, please, whether you were able to establish how far the police building was from this building?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: I don't really know. And as far as I can recall, we did not consider that to be very relevant to the incident, itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, don't you think that it was necessary to establish, in view of the fact that the uniformed police took part in combat, that the police station building was an important feature in view of the fact that it could be treated as a military target?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: In the vicinity of the building that I indicated was a residential building, there was nothing that I could observe as being the police station, and I also was not able to observe that in the vicinity of this residential building and this apartment where this one individual was killed, that any other apartments in the neighbourhood were used as military installations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm familiar with that name. And as far as I know, it's in the area of the new part of town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the interpreters were not able to hear your last question, i.e., the name of something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Refika Sokolara Street, are you familiar with that? If I tell you that Refik Sokolar, during his testimony, testified that there was a police station on that street, would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: I don't know what he confirmed or what his statement was, and I really can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please have 1D215.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was the name of the witness you referred to, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The police officer's name was Refik Sokolar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know that this police officer's name, Refik Sokolar, can be found in reference to at least two incidents and maybe more?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. And as far as my work was concerned, I never came across it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 1D2151, please. It's a map. This is not the document that we see now. This is not what I was asking for. Could we zoom in on the area indicated as "Dobrinja," because I would like the witness to mark some things there. Is it possible to focus this a little better? We can't make out the street names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If we zoom out, then we may be able to see the names. No. This is a scanned version, and the quality of the map is not that good as one can expect. That's what I'm told.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can use a different map from the Prosecution binder. Could we have 65 ter 19089. My apologies, 65 ter 13581.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sheet number 10, Exhibit P1739.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe we can zoom this in without losing the sharp image. Could we just have before us Dobrinja, itself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, would you please mark Miroslava Krleze Street. You can see the street name right here. It is indicated on the map, itself.

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, it's right here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We zoom out again. Before you go on, we need to zoom out. Just wait a minute. Move to the left a bit. Further, further, and going up. Is it okay?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Could you mark the street? We should zoom out. Fine, fine. Now go to the left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Change to the pencil.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. You have to push the arrow first and then move the map to the left. Further, yes, going up. Yes, I think it's okay now. Go down, a bit down. Further. Yes. Too much? Yes, yes. Let's start.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please mark Miroslava Krleze Street and the building of the incident.

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: [Marks]. I don't think it was on Miroslava Krleze Street. I think the incident involving one victim was in Nehruova Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see Hamdije Kapidzica Street?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you mark the building now?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: I've already said that I'm not very familiar with this part of town, especially not at that time. But as far as I can see on this map, there are two buildings on that street, and I will indicate both of them, if that's all right [marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I remind you. You said in your report that the room where the young woman was killed was facing south-east; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you established that the round had come from Miroslava Krleze Street; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that one of the referent damages to the facility was on the curtain, itself? That's in paragraph 19 of your statement, on page 5.

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Well, first, it says that there was some damage on the left part of the window, 116 centimetres from the floor, where there was a bullet hole where the bullet had entered, and the same kind of damage or hole was found on the curtain, 116.5 centimetres from the floor, and also on the wardrobe, and the distance between the various points where the bullet struck were some 20 centimetres on the wall, behind the wardrobe. We recovered the round on the floor, and there were traces of blood found on the bedside and on parts of the floor. And, yes, that's what it says in my report, and there's also mention made of the hole in the curtain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 19, you also said that there was a hole in the curtain, but then earlier on you said that you need two reference points in order to be able to determine the direction of the projectile, the incoming projectile?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: I said earlier that I never claimed anything as regards the direction of the fire, but as you can see from the report, the scene-of-crime officer was able to find a number of holes or damages incurred by the bullet. So it was not just a hole in the curtain, but also a number of other holes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in paragraph 19, you mention only two of those? One of them was on the window frame, a plastic sheet on it, and the other end was in the curtains?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned the plastic sheet because it was actually attached to the window, and it was there to replace the window-pane. The second one was on the curtain, and the third reference point was on the wardrobe. And then if you draw a line and connect all these three points, then you could draw a certain conclusion. So I am repeating again: There was not just one such reference point on -- there was another one on the curtain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your report, you mention two different parts. These two different parts or two different areas are, in any case, either the curtain or the plastic sheet of the window, and this ballistics expertise was actually carried out by a scene-of-crime officer and not by a ballistics expert; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if you can call it "expertise," but on the basis of everything that is stated here in the report, the scene-of-crime officer determined the direction. As for any details in that respect, I believe you should ask him about it. I only accepted the information that he provided to me on the site, itself. We should look at his report and see what method he applied in order to determine that the bullet had come from that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what floor was this apartment on?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: If it's not mentioned in the report, I can't really recall it. I will try to find and see whether that was mentioned in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was on the fourth floor; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here, the fourth floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, please take a look at the map. Between Miroslava Krleze Street and the two buildings on Hamdije Kapidzica Street, are there any buildings in between that are taller than four storeys?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that I'm not very familiar with the area. I don't know if there are any other buildings that are higher than four storeys.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, tell us, you said that the room where the incident occurred faced south-east; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that this part of the building actually faces west-south-west? Would you please draw a perpendicular line in relation to these two buildings, or, rather, the closest one to Hamdije Kapidzica Street. So could you draw a perpendicular line in relation to the street between the two buildings?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure -- I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the closest -- the closer of the two buildings on Hamdije Kapidzica Street, would you draw a perpendicular line?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is not a perpendicular line. Would you please make a right angle in relation to the street there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand what you're asking me to do. What do you mean "right angle"? Right angle to what? In relation to the building on Hamdije Kapidzica Street or in relation to Miroslava Krleze Street? Which building?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let me explain it. Do you agree with me that when we say you need a perpendicular line, that means that there is a right angle --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We do not need the assistance of the witness to see how a perpendicular line to that building would look like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that a perpendicular line, in relation to that building, would actually be -- would face south-west and not south-east?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Are you referring to the building on Hamdije Kapidzica Street?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the building where the incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Well, if you want me to mark approximately where the south-east is in relation to the building on Hamdije Kapidzica Street, I can do that. That is in the direction, roughly, of the airport runway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The rooms on this side in this building, do they face south-east or south-west?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Well, I would say south-west, which is not to say that they do not face south-east as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you said they faced south-east, and here we see that this apartment is actually facing south-west.

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Well, I'm not really such an expert to determine exactly where south-west or south-east on this map would be. I may have made an error, and I may be corrected, but that's what it says in the report, that it is in the direction of Miroslava Krleze Street. If that is not south-east, then that's just another way of saying that it faces Miroslava Krleze Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please sign and date this document.

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Delete the signature part, and why don't you put your witness number, which is "KDZ485." So we delete that signature. Shall we ask the witness to delete the lines between the buildings and the street or shall we leave it as it is?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the mistake made here. I think we should erase this, perhaps, and draw a perpendicular line pointing to this building, or leave it empty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We just delete the line you draw between the two markings. Yes. Could you put "KDZ485"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be admitted ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D861, Your Honours. And for the record, MFI D859 will be under seal. That's 1D2721.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you participated in investigating an incident of the 22nd December 1994 in a part of Bascarsija known as "flea market"?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That incident happened at 10 past 9.00, and you made your report and signed it. Can we see 65 ter 09721 - it's page 3 in Serbian - without broadcasting it, please. What was the weather like that morning; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: I can't remember, but I will try to see if it's in the report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 09721, page 3, without broadcasting. And there's a translation as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I only note that -- perhaps we can quickly move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did say it shouldn't be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we announced that exhibit number. I know what you mean. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you also need to see the page before, Witness?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: If that's the page with names, the names of the members of the team and the commission, then, no, I have it before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it the case, if you are informed, that members of the police and members of the BH Army rushed to help the injured at that moment?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: I can't remember that now. But if it's in the report, then it's true. Right now, I can't remember. I'll try to find it in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's not in the report. I'm quoting from some evidence. Can we see 65 ter 13172. 13172, page 70. Because this has been exhibited and the witness has refreshed his memory, we can remove this document. How do you explain the presence of police officers, and especially of the members of the Armed Forces of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so quickly on the site? In English, it's page 21. You can see the name of this witness and his signature. In the second paragraph, line 16, you find what I've just said. I believe in English it's perhaps on the next page. Do you see, line 16, that the police and members of the BH Army came to their rescue immediately? Yes, it says so there, to help the wounded -- in English, it's the second line from the top. "... to help the wounded, followed by policemen and members of the BH Army."

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: I do not know what this witness says. I did not see policemen or army members on-site when I came. Perhaps that person, the person who gave the statement, can explain. I have no explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you secure these witnesses, because it's your duty to secure the witnesses so they can give the statements?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Well, the statements were taken from my colleagues from a different department called the Genocide Department. I just took their names.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we have some time left, we'll talk about that genocide. But before that, I'd like to tender this document, unless it's already a Prosecution exhibit. Sorry, it's D554, and it's already exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a sketch made by the members of your team?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Regarding this incident? No, I don't remember if that sketch ever reached me. A sketch is normally made by the scene-of-crime officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you know that scene because you participated in the investigation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Yes, I roughly remember the scene. If you could show me a photograph, that would help me remember the details, but I know approximately where it happened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 17 of this document. We can remove the rest, the document on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the scene, Telali Street? It used to be Petar Kocic Street, and the other street is Oprkanj Street. It used to be Danila Ilica Street.

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
utterances.text: Yes, that's approximately that place, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that the spots where two persons lost their lives are not marked?

utterances.speaker: KDZ485
